analogy.p: Classification is like a postal address that narrows from country to town to street to house: kingdom is the country, species is the house number, and the more of the address two organisms share, the closer together they live on the tree of life. An evolutionary tree is like a family tree of streets, showing which houses were built from the same plan. It breaks down because addresses are chosen by humans while evolutionary relationships are discovered from evidence and can be revised.

bullets: **Linnaean system:** kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
**Binomial system:** two-part Latin name, **genus** then **species**.
Classification models **changed** because of better **microscopes** and understanding of **biochemical processes**.
**Three-domain system** (Woese): **archaea, bacteria, eukaryota**.
**Evolutionary trees** show how scientists **believe** organisms are related, using **classification data** and **fossil data**.
Links: **theories of evolution**, **fossils**, **speciation**, **DNA and genetics**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.6.4 Classification of living organisms asks you to know how living things are **traditionally classified into groups by their structure and characteristics** in the system developed by **Carl Linnaeus**, how organisms are **named by the binomial system**, why **models of classification have changed**, what the **three-domain system** of **Carl Woese** is, and how **evolutionary trees** show relationships. It matters because classification is how biologists organise millions of species, and because it links directly to evolution: organisms grouped together are grouped because they are closely related.

bullets: Classification gives scientists a **common language**, so a species has the same name worldwide.
It makes it easier to **identify** unknown organisms and to **predict** their features from their group.
It shows **relationships**: members of the same group are likely to share a **recent common ancestor**.
It helps with **conservation**, because we need to know what species exist and how distinct they are.
Early classification used **physical (structural) characteristics** only, as that was what could be observed.
Link to **variation** and **evolution**: shared features are inherited from common ancestors.
core.p: There are millions of species, and scientists need an agreed way to group them so that they can communicate clearly, identify organisms, and understand how they are related. Classification sorts organisms into groups on the basis of the **characteristics they share**. Traditionally these are **observable features of structure**, such as having a backbone, feathers, or flowers. The more characteristics two organisms share, the more closely related they are thought to be and the more groups they share.

bullets: The order from largest to smallest: **kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**.
Memory aid: **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ood **S**oup.
Kingdom is the **broadest** group (e.g. animals); species is the **most specific**.
Example, a human: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, Homo sapiens.
Example, a lion: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, Panthera, Panthera leo.
Lion and human share the **kingdom, phylum and class** but are different in order, so they are less closely related than a lion and tiger.
You need to **recall the seven levels in order**, but you are not expected to memorise the names of orders or families.
core.p: Carl Linnaeus developed a system that classifies organisms into a **hierarchy of seven groups**. The biggest group is the **kingdom** and the smallest is the **species**. Each level is nested inside the one above, like folders inside folders. As you move down the hierarchy the groups get **smaller** and contain **fewer organisms**, but the members of each group have **more characteristics in common**.

bullets: Species = organisms that can **interbreed to produce fertile offspring**.
Horse × donkey = mule, which is **infertile**, so they are different species.
The species definition has limits: it does not work for **asexual organisms** like many bacteria, or for **fossils**.
Species in the same genus are closely related and share a **recent common ancestor**.
New species form by **speciation**: isolation, natural selection acting differently, and eventually inability to interbreed.
Link to **natural selection** and **genetic variation**.
core.p: The species is the base unit of Linnaean classification. Although the specification does not give a formal definition here, in GCSE terms a **species is a group of organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring**. For example, a horse and a donkey can mate to produce a mule, but a mule is sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species. This idea links to **speciation** in the evolution topic: when two populations become so different they can no longer interbreed, they have become new species.

bullets: **Genus** comes first and starts with a **capital letter**; **species** comes second and is all **lower case**.
Written in **italics** when printed, or **underlined** when handwritten.
Example: Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) share the genus **Panthera**, so they are closely related.
Different organisms never share exactly the same binomial name.
A shared genus tells you the species are **closely related** and probably share a recent common ancestor.
Advantage: **universal**, avoids confusion caused by **local common names**.
In the exam: if asked to write the binomial name, give both parts in the right order and format.
core.p: Linnaeus also introduced the **binomial system**, in which every organism is given a **two-part Latin name**. The **first part is the genus** and the **second part is the species**. For example, humans are Homo sapiens, where Homo is the genus and sapiens the species. Binomial names are used because common names vary between languages and places (a 'robin' in Britain is a different bird from the 'robin' in America), whereas the scientific name is **the same everywhere in the world**.

bullets: Improved **microscopes** revealed **internal structures** such as cell structure and organelles.
Better understanding of **biochemical processes** allowed comparison of **molecules** (e.g. proteins, DNA, RNA).
Organisms that look similar may be **unrelated** (similar adaptations), while organisms that look different may be **closely related**.
New evidence therefore led to **new models** being proposed and tested by the scientific community.
This shows that science is **tentative**: models change when **new evidence** conflicts with them.
Link to **How Science Works**: peer review, repeatability, and evidence-led change.
core.h: Why models of classification have changed
core.p: Scientific models are **improved as new evidence is found**, and classification is a good example. Linnaeus based his system on what could be **seen with the naked eye or simple microscopes**: structure and characteristics. As **microscopes improved**, scientists could see the **internal structures** of cells, and discovered that some organisms (like bacteria) have no nucleus. As the **understanding of biochemical processes progressed**, scientists could compare organisms' **chemistry**, such as their proteins and DNA. These new kinds of evidence showed that some groupings based on appearance did not reflect true evolutionary relationships.

bullets: **Archaea:** primitive bacteria, usually living in **extreme environments** such as hot springs, salt lakes or deep sea vents.
**Bacteria:** **true bacteria** (the ones that cause infections, such as Staphylococcus, as well as many harmless ones).
**Eukaryota:** includes **protists, fungi, plants and animals**.
Archaea and bacteria are both **prokaryotes** (no nucleus) but chemical analysis shows they are very different.
Eukaryotes have cells with a **nucleus** and other membrane-bound organelles.
The three-domain system sits **above** the Linnaean kingdoms; the kingdoms of eukaryota are protists, fungi, plants and animals.
Name Woese correctly: **Carl Woese** (three domains) versus **Carl Linnaeus** (seven-level hierarchy and binomials).
core.p: Because of evidence from **chemical analysis**, a new model called the **three-domain system** was developed by **Carl Woese**. A **domain** is a level **above kingdom**, so it is the largest grouping. Organisms are divided into **three domains**: **archaea**, **bacteria** and **eukaryota**. This system shows that what were once all called 'bacteria' fall into two very different groups (archaea and true bacteria), and that all organisms with a nucleus belong in one domain.

bullets: Linnaeus: **structure and characteristics**; Woese: **chemical analysis** (as well as newer evidence).
Linnaeus: 7 levels from kingdom to species; Woese: 3 **domains**.
Linnaeus: bacteria were grouped as one; Woese: bacteria split into **archaea** and **bacteria**.
Both are **hierarchies** that group organisms by relatedness.
Both models are **provisional** and can change with new evidence.
Exam tip: link each system to the **type of evidence** it used.
core.h: Comparing the Linnaean and three-domain systems
core.p: Good answers explain what each system is based on and why the second was adopted. The **Linnaean** system is based mainly on **observable structure and characteristics**, whereas the **three-domain** system uses **chemical evidence**. The three-domain system does not replace the seven levels; it adds a **higher level** and re-arranges the very top of the tree of life, especially for microorganisms.

bullets: Each **branching point (node)** represents a **common ancestor**.
Two species that split **recently** share a recent common ancestor and are **closely related**.
Species that split **long ago** are **more distantly related**.
**Extinct** organisms (known only from fossils) can be included, often shown with dashed lines or marked as extinct.
Trees show **belief based on evidence**, so they can be **redrawn** when new fossils or DNA data appear.
The **length of a branch** may or may not show time; check the question for a time axis.
core.p: An **evolutionary tree** is a diagram that shows how scientists **believe** different organisms are related. The branching pattern shows **common ancestors**. Where two branches split, there was a **common ancestor** of the two groups. The closer together two organisms are on the tree (the more recent their split), the more **closely related** they are. Trees are built from **current classification data for living organisms** (structures, DNA, chemistry) and **fossil data for extinct organisms**.

bullets: Start at each species and move **towards the root** until the lines join; that join is the **common ancestor**.
The pair that joins **closest to the tips** is the **most closely related**.
Two species on opposite sides of the **first split** are the most distantly related.
Species on the tips did not evolve **from each other**; they evolved from a **shared common ancestor**.
The root represents the **oldest ancestor** shown on the tree.
Count branches carefully: some questions ask how many **species** there are, how many **common ancestors**.
core.h: How to read an evolutionary tree
core.p: Exam questions usually ask you to identify which two species are most closely related, which is the oldest common ancestor, or whether a species could be an ancestor of another. Always trace **back along the branches** to find the point where two lines meet. The **most recent junction** tells you who is most closely related. Remember that living species are at the **tips** of branches and are not ancestors of each other: they are 'cousins' who share a common ancestor.

bullets: **Fossil data** for extinct organisms and dating of when groups arose.
**Current classification data** for living organisms (structure and characteristics).
**DNA/chemical analysis**: fewer differences in sequences = more recent common ancestor.
Fossil record is **incomplete** (soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise), so trees have gaps.
New discoveries can **change** the tree, which shows that science is evidence-led.
Link to **Evidence for evolution** (fossils, DNA, anatomy).
core.h: Sources of data used to build trees
core.p: Scientists draw evolutionary trees using several types of evidence. **Fossils** give the structure and age of extinct organisms and show **when** groups appeared. **Comparative anatomy** compares structures of living organisms. **Chemical and molecular data**, such as the sequence of bases in DNA and the structure of proteins, give detailed information on relatedness: the more similar the DNA, the more closely related the organisms. Together these produce more reliable trees than any one source alone.

bullets: Shared characteristics are **homologous**: inherited from a common ancestor (e.g. the pentadactyl limb in mammals; extension only).
**Speciation** produces new species, which appear as new branches.
**Extinction** ends branches; the fossil record shows extinct groups.
**Selective breeding and genetic engineering** are not classification but are related by genetics.
**Resistant bacteria** are an example of evolution happening rapidly.
Higher tier links: use evolutionary language such as 'common ancestor' and 'diverged' in 6 mark answers.
core.h: Links to evolution, speciation and fossils
core.p: Classification and evolutionary trees are the visible result of **evolution by natural selection**. Organisms that share a recent common ancestor have inherited many of the same features and alleles. When populations become isolated and diverge through **speciation**, new branches are added to the tree. **Fossils** fill in the extinct branches, and **extinction** removes whole lines of descent. So the tree of life can be thought of as a record of **common descent**.

bullets: Say 'closely related' = 'shares a **recent common ancestor**'.
Say 'classification models change because **new evidence** becomes available'.
Mention **internal structures** when talking about microscopes and **chemical analysis** for Woese.
Do **not** say 'monkeys evolved into humans': both share a common ancestor.
Spell the domains correctly: **archaea, bacteria, eukaryota** (archaea is not 'archaebacteria' on AQA).
Remember: **Linnaeus = hierarchy and binomial**; **Woese = three domains**.
core.p: Examiners reward precise vocabulary. Use words from the specification wording and avoid vague phrases such as 'evolved from' when you mean 'shared a common ancestor'. When asked why classification changed, always name the **type of new evidence** (better microscopes or chemical analysis) and say that it showed **new information** that did not fit the old model. When asked about naming, mention **genus** and **species** and that the name is the same worldwide.

exam: **Recall (1-2 marks):** state the seven Linnaean levels in order, name the three domains, or state that binomial names have genus then species.
**Describe the binomial system (2 marks):** 'two-part name' + 'genus and species' (+ 'same name worldwide').
**Explain why classification changed (3-4 marks):** new evidence → improved microscopes showed internal structures → biochemical/chemical analysis → new model (three domains) proposed.
**Evolutionary tree questions:** find the **most recent common ancestor**; the pair joined closest to the tips are the most closely related.
**'Suggest' questions:** use 'closely related' and 'common ancestor' vocabulary, not 'evolved from'.
**Distinguish models:** Linnaeus used **structure and characteristics**; Woese used **chemical analysis** and made **three domains**.
**Data questions:** if given DNA similarity percentages, the higher the similarity, the more closely related.
**Naming:** italics or underline, capital letter for genus only.
**6 mark questions** may combine classification, fossils and evolution; link them with 'common ancestor'.
**Use the words** 'believe' or 'suggest' when talking about evolutionary trees, because they are models.

mistakes.r: **Woese** proposed the three-domain system; **Linnaeus** developed the seven-level system and binomial names.
**Genus first with a capital letter**, **species second in lower case**: Homo sapiens (italic or underlined).
mistakes.w: Genus and species written in any order, any case: homo Sapiens.

mistakes.r: Because of **new evidence**: better **microscopes** (internal structures) and **chemical analysis**/biochemical understanding.
mistakes.w: Classification changed because scientists changed their minds.

mistakes.r: Archaea are **primitive bacteria in extreme environments**; bacteria are **true bacteria**; they are different domains.
mistakes.w: Archaea are the same as bacteria.

mistakes.r: Humans and chimpanzees **share a common ancestor**; neither evolved from the other.
They show how scientists **believe** organisms are related, based on current data and fossils, and can change.
mistakes.w: Evolutionary trees prove how organisms are related.

mistakes.r: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species, from **largest to smallest**.
mistakes.w: Order of levels given as species, genus ... or mixed up.

mistakes.r: Organisms in the same genus are **different, closely related species**.
mistakes.w: Organisms in the same genus are the same species.

summary: The specification asks you to know the Linnaean hierarchy and binomial naming, why classification models changed with better microscopes and chemical analysis, the three-domain system of Woese, and how evolutionary trees show how scientists believe organisms are related. It matters because classification and trees are the organising framework for evolution and biodiversity.

terms.d: Sorting living organisms into groups based on their structure and characteristics (and now chemical evidence).
A system of classification developed by Carl Linnaeus using kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
The largest group in the Linnaean system, such as animals, plants, fungi.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A group of closely related species; the first part of the binomial name.
A naming system using two parts: the genus followed by the species.
The largest classification group in the three-domain system.
A model of classification developed by Carl Woese dividing organisms into archaea, bacteria and eukaryota.
Primitive bacteria, usually living in extreme environments.
True bacteria; prokaryotic organisms such as those causing infections.
The domain that includes protists, fungi, plants and animals; cells have a nucleus.
A diagram that shows how scientists believe organisms are related.
An organism from which two or more different groups have evolved.
No longer existing; a species with no living members.
The remains of organisms from millions of years ago, found in rocks.
A single-celled organism with no nucleus, such as bacteria and archaea.
An arrangement in which groups are nested inside larger groups.

worked.ans: Homo sapiens (underlined or italic). Homo is the genus; sapiens is the species.
worked.q: Write the binomial name of humans in the correct format and state what each part represents. (3 marks)
steps: Genus first with capital letter: Homo.
Species second, all lower case: sapiens.

worked.ans: B. A and B share a more recent common ancestor than A shares with C or D.
worked.q: The diagram shows an evolutionary tree of species A, B, C and D. A and B split from each other more recently than from C and D. State which species is most closely related to A and explain your answer. (2 marks)
steps: Trace A back to where its line meets another.
It meets B first (most recent common ancestor).

worked.ans: Originally organisms were classified by structure and characteristics. Improved microscopes revealed internal structures, and better understanding of biochemical processes allowed chemical analysis. This new evidence did not fit the old model, so Carl Woese proposed the three-domain system of archaea, bacteria and eukaryota.
worked.q: Explain why scientists have changed the way they classify living organisms. (4 marks)
steps: Linnaeus classified by structure and characteristics.
Understanding of biochemical processes grew, allowing chemical analysis.
New evidence led to a new model: the three-domain system proposed by Woese.
